records.name: Stella
records.facts_used: Stella: The name belongs to the Stella / Estelle / Estella family. Its linguistic basis is explained through Latin stella, star; Estella is a Latinate form of Estelle. The historical connection survives changes of spelling and endings across languages. The beginning of a particular local form’s use must be distinguished from the earlier history of the whole family. Stella is also the literary name in Philip Sidney’s sonnet sequence Astrophil and Stella. Folger’s manuscript catalogue dates the sequence’s first London publication to 1591. This is an English literary example, rather than the first Stella registration in Latvia or every family’s reason for choosing the name.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.

records.name: Zvaigznīte
records.facts_used: Zvaigznīte: The Latvian dictionary explains the name’s formation through Zvaigzne and a diminutive form; Latvian zvaigzne means star. This is a specific connection with Latvian vocabulary. The explanation concerns the form discussed in the dictionary; similar spellings require their own origin and attestation checks. Siliņš’s dictionary dates the use of Zvaigznīte: possibly 1973. This records use of the particular name in Latvia. The entry cannot automatically be transferred to similar spellings or treated as the moment the entire name family originated.

records.name: Eugenija
records.facts_used: Eugenija: The name belongs to the Eugenia / Eugenija / Eugenius family. Its linguistic basis is explained through Greek eugenēs, well born, from eu and genēs. The historical connection survives changes of spelling and endings across languages. The beginning of a particular local form’s use must be distinguished from the earlier history of the whole family. The 1964 calendar reprinted in Salys’s 1983 volume gives Eugenija (Genė) on 25 December. This is a concrete printed example of the form’s use. Its position in the historical calendar need not match every modern calendar and is not the name’s invention date.
